summary: 10. The Petitioners, in their rejoinder dated 8.2.2023, to the reply filed by CTUIL, reiterated the submissions made in the petition, besides the following submissions: b) CTUIL’s reliance on Petition No. 293/MP/2015, Jaiprakash Power Ventures v. PGCIL, is misplaced because in this case, the Commission had held that the _(b) The Petitioners and CTUIL to convene a meeting to clarify and confirm the details of the billing. Thereafter, the Petitioners shall file an affidavit within a week, giving the details of the minutes of meeting and the details of the bills raised._ _"...2. The Commission directed the Petitioner and CTUIL to comply with the directions given in the RoP for the hearing dated 24.1.2023 wherein the Petitioners and CTUIL were directed to convene a meeting to clarify and confirm the details of the billing and to file an affidavit within 10 days, giving the details of the minutes of meeting and details of the bills raised."_ _“20. Next, we now proceed to examine the prayers made in the Petition and the underlying issue(s) involved therein in light of the ratio laid down in the DVC judgement. On bare perusal of the prayers as well as grounds raised in the Petition, we note that the main prayer of the Petitioner was to hold and declare that the PPA stands terminated on account of force majeure and impossibility in terms of Article 4.5.3 read with Article 13.5 with effect from 05.02.2022 or in the alternate, hold and declare that the PPA stands frustrated on account of force majeure and impossibility of performance in terms of Section 56 of the Indian Contract Act, 1872. All other reliefs are ancillary or consequential in nature. Thus, the main issue is whether the PPA is legally and validly terminated. We observe that, as per the ratio emerging from the DVC judgment dated 28.8.2024, such issues cannot be termed as ‘tariff disputes’ and, as a result, the adjudicatory jurisdiction of this Commission under Section 79(1)(f) read with Section 79(1)(b) does not extend to such disputes.”_ _“27. As already noted in the foregoing paragraphs, the main dispute in the Petition is of the termination of PPA on the part of the Petitioner. As already held by the APTEL in the DVC judgement that the dispute relating to termination of a PPA is confined to the legality and validity of the termination of PPA and does not relate to tariff or regulation of tariff, therefore, the issue involved in the present case also cannot be guised as a tariff dispute. The prayer seeking directions of reimbursement of_ _(i) The primary/principal dispute involved the Petitioner and Respondents in the present Petition does not relate to tariff or regulation of tariff and such dispute, thus, does not fall within the ambit of adjudicatory jurisdiction of this Commission under Section 79(1)(f) read with Section 79(1)(b) of the Act._ _(ii) As a result, the Commission is bound to refer such disputes to the arbitration in terms of the latter part of Section 79(1)(f) of the Act as the expression “and to refer any dispute for arbitration” used therein, as explained in DVC Judgment, definitely leaves scope for some disputes to be referred to the arbitration._ _(iii) Timely invocation of Section 8 of the A & C Act is not a prerequisite for this Commission to refer the disputes to the arbitration, especially when such disputes are beyond the adjudicatory jurisdiction of the Commission under Section 79(1)(f) read with Section 79(1)(b), as have been in this Petition._ _Keeping in view the nature of the dispute and the value involved in the Petition, the Commission finds it appropriate to refer the dispute(s) between the contracting parties to a panel comprising three arbitrators as per Regulation 49(b) of the COB Regulations, 2023. Accordingly, both the contracting parties shall suggest the names of the arbitrators in terms of the said Regulation within two weeks from the date of this order, and the third arbitrator shall be nominated based on the suggestions of both the nominated arbitrators.”_ Further, in the order dated 8.6.2022 in Petition No. 103/MP/2021, the Commission has held as follows: 33. The Petitioners have relied upon the judgment of the Hon’ble Supreme Court in Ameet Lalchand Shah v. Rishabh Enterprises, (2018) 15 SCC 678. We have considered the said reliance. In the Ameet Lalchand Shah case. The issue before the Hon’ble Supreme Court in that matter pertained to whether the disputes arising under multiple agreements forming part of a single commercial project could be referred to 37. Accordingly, Issue No. 1 is decided against the Petitioners. **Issue No. 2: Whether the Petitioners are liable to pay the transmission charges from the date of operationalisation of the LTA (Tranche 1 and Tranche 2)?** _4.0 This Order shall be applied prospectively i.e. from the date of issue of Order.”_ _78. The Petitioner is directed to make payments of the bills raised by CTUIL in accordance with directions under this Order as per Regulations. Issue No.4 is answered accordingly and prayer (f) of the Petitioner is rejected.”_
